title: Common-Source Stage
intro: The common-source (CS) stage is the basic voltage amplifier: the input drives the gate and the output is taken at the drain. This page covers the resistor-loaded stage in detail (Razavi, Section 3.3.1); other loads and degeneration have their own pages.

blocks.text: Large-signal behaviour

blocks.alt: Schematic of a common-source amplifier. An NMOS transistor M1 has its source grounded, its gate driven by the input Vin and its drain connected through a resistor RD to the supply VDD. The output Vout is taken at the drain.
blocks.caption: A common-source stage with a resistor load.

blocks.text: Sweep $V_{in}$ upward. Below $V_{TH}$, M1 is off and $V_{out} = V_{DD}$. Just above threshold M1 must be saturated (its drain is far above its gate), so

As $V_{out}$ falls it eventually drops one threshold below the gate, $V_{out} = V_{in} - V_{TH}$ (point A), and M1 enters triode. At point A the equation above holds with $V_{out} = V_{in1} - V_{TH}$, which can be solved for $V_{in1}$. Further on, the triode equation applies, and deep in triode M1 is just $R_{on}$ in a divider:

blocks.alt: Two plots against input voltage from 0 to 1.8 volts. Top: output voltage stays at 1.8 volts until the input reaches 0.5 volts, then falls along a parabola to point A near 1.23 volts input and 0.73 volts output, marked as the edge of triode, then decays slowly toward about 0.3 volts. Bottom: the small-signal gain magnitude is zero below 0.5 volts, rises linearly to a peak of about 2.9 at point A, then drops quickly in triode.
blocks.caption: Transfer curve and gain of a CS stage. The gain is largest just before M1 leaves saturation, and the stage is biased to the left of point A.

blocks.text: Small-signal gain
In saturation the slope of the transfer curve is

blocks.tex: A_v = \frac{\partial V_{out}}{\partial V_{in}} = -R_D\,\mu_n C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}(V_{in} - V_{TH}) = -g_m R_D

blocks.text: The same result follows from the small-signal model: an input change produces a drain current $g_m v_{in}$, which flows through $R_D$. Because $g_m$ itself depends on $V_{in}$, the gain changes with signal level when the swing is large: that is nonlinearity. A recurring design idea follows: make the gain depend as little as possible on signal-dependent quantities like $g_m$.

Driven hard enough to swing between cutoff and triode, the device's $g_m$ (and so the incremental gain) varies periodically with the signal: near zero when the input is low, largest at the saturation edge, small again in triode.
Maximizing the gain
Write $g_m = \sqrt{2\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)I_D}$ and $R_D = V_{RD}/I_D$, where $V_{RD}$ is the DC drop across $R_D$:

items: Larger $W/L$: more gain, but more device capacitance.
Larger $V_{RD}$: more gain, but less room for swing. If $V_{DD} - V_{RD}$ falls to $V_{in} - V_{TH}$ the device sits at the triode edge with no swing left.
Smaller $I_D$ at fixed $V_{RD}$: more gain, but $R_D$ grows and the output node becomes slower.
So gain trades with bandwidth and swing, and a lower supply tightens all three.

blocks.text: Including channel-length modulation
With $\lambda > 0$ the transistor's $r_o$ sits in parallel with $R_D$ (differentiating the large-signal equation with the $(1+\lambda V_{out})$ factor gives the same answer, with more effort):

Replace $R_D$ by an ideal current source and the gain becomes the intrinsic gain $-g_m r_o$, the most a single transistor can give (only about 5 to 10 in modern short-channel devices). Note that $R_D$ cannot simply be removed to raise the gain: the bias current needs a path from the supply. In the current-source-loaded stage, how does $V_{in}$ change the drain current if the current is fixed? It doesn't: $I_D = \frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)(V_{in} - V_{TH})^2(1 + \lambda V_{out})$ stays equal to the source current, so $V_{out}$ moves to compensate. Loosely saying the current rises with $V_{in}$ refers to the squared term only.
Any terminal that controls the channel can be the input: driving the bulk with the gate at a fixed bias gives $A_v = -g_{mb}R_D$ (with $\lambda = 0$), a smaller gain because $g_{mb} < g_m$.

The steepest part of the curve, between threshold and the triode edge, is the amplifying region. Increase $R_D$ and the slope steepens (more gain) but the usable input range shrinks: the gain-swing trade-off in one picture.
Other versions

Resistors are often imprecise or large on chip, so the load is usually a transistor: diode-connected, current-source, active (complementary) or triode loads, each on the CS Stage with Transistor Loads page. Adding a resistor in the source gives the degenerated stage on the Source Degeneration page.

blocks.title: Gain with and without ro
blocks.text: $g_m = 1\text{ mS}$, $R_D = 10\text{ k}\Omega$, $r_o = 50\text{ k}\Omega$. Find the CS gain with $r_o$ ignored and with it included.

blocks.title: The edge of triode
blocks.text: A CS stage has $V_{DD} = 1.8\text{ V}$, $R_D = 2\text{ k}\Omega$, $\mu_n C_{ox}W/L = 2\text{ mA/V}^2$, $V_{TH} = 0.5\text{ V}$ and $\lambda = 0$. Find the input voltage at which M1 enters triode, the output there, and the small-signal gain at that point.
blocks.hint: Set $V_{out} = V_{in} - V_{TH}$ in the saturation equation.
solution: At the edge $V_{out} = V_{in} - V_{TH} = V_{ov}$, so $V_{ov} = 1.8 - 2\text{ k}\Omega \cdot 1\text{ mA/V}^2 \cdot V_{ov}^2$, i.e. $2V_{ov}^2 + V_{ov} - 1.8 = 0$.
blocks.answer: $V_{in1} \approx 1.23\text{ V}$, $V_{out} \approx 0.73\text{ V}$, $|A_v| \approx 2.9$ (the peak in the figure).

blocks.title: Deep in triode
blocks.text: For the same stage, estimate $V_{out}$ at $V_{in} = 1.8\text{ V}$ with the $R_{on}$ approximation, then check with the full triode equation.
solution: Full triode: $V_{out} = 1.8 - 4(1.3V_{out} - V_{out}^2/2)$, i.e. $2V_{out}^2 - 6.2V_{out} + 1.8 = 0$, giving $V_{out} \approx 0.32\text{ V}$. The $R_{on}$ estimate is about 10 percent low because $V_{out}$ is only about 8 times smaller than $2V_{ov} = 2.6\text{ V}$, so the squared term is not negligible.

blocks.title: Trading current for gain
blocks.text: A CS stage has $\mu_n C_{ox}W/L = 1\text{ mA/V}^2$ and 0.6 V across $R_D$ at $I_D = 100\,\mu\text{A}$. Find the gain. Keeping $V_{RD}$ fixed, what happens if $I_D$ is halved?
solution: Halving $I_D$ multiplies $|A_v|$ by $\sqrt{2}$, to 3.79, but $R_D$ doubles to $12\text{ k}\Omega$, so the output pole moves down by about half.
blocks.answer: 2.68, rising to 3.79 at half the current (with a slower output node).
